title: Whistler, Arc Trips
hero_lede: Whistler is best known for Whistler Blackcomb, skiing, snowboarding, the Peak 2 Peak Gondola, Whistler Village, mountain biking, alpine hiking, lakes, and après-ski.

items.name: Lost Lake Loop
items.alt: A forested lake with a small island
paras: The main Lost Lake loop is about 4 km, with minimal elevation gain, and usually takes 1 to 1.5 hours at a relaxed pace. You can also add nearby forest trails if you want a longer walk.
This area is beautiful in summer, when people swim, picnic, and bike nearby. In winter, Lost Lake becomes a Nordic skiing and snowshoeing area, so trail access changes by season.
items.note: Lost Lake can be busy in summer. Go early or later in the day if you want a quieter walk.

items.name: Whistler Valley Trail
items.alt: Cyclists on the Valley Trail beside the lake
paras: The Whistler Valley Trail is not a wilderness hike, but it is one of the easiest and most useful walking routes in Whistler. This paved trail network connects Whistler Village, parks, lakes, neighborhoods, viewpoints, and picnic areas.

You can walk just a short section or make it a longer outing. Since the trail is mostly flat and paved, it is good for families, casual walkers, strollers, bikes, and visitors who do not want a rough trail.

Distances vary depending on your route. A short walk may take 30 minutes, while a longer lake-to-lake route can take several hours. Elevation gain is usually minimal, making this one of the easiest ways to explore Whistler on foot.
items.note: This is a shared trail, so watch for cyclists, children, dogs, and other walkers.

items.name: Train Wreck Trail
paras: Train Wreck is one of the most unique hikes in Whistler. The trail leads through forest to old painted train boxcars scattered near the Cheakamus River. It also crosses a suspension-style bridge, making the hike more memorable.

The Train Wreck hike is about 5 km round trip, with minimal elevation gain, and usually takes 1 to 3 hours, depending on how long you spend exploring and taking photos. It is an easy hike, but there are roots, forest paths, and some uneven sections.
This is a good choice if you want a short hike with something different from the usual lake or mountain viewpoint.
items.note: Use the official trail access. Do not walk on railway tracks.

items.name: Rainbow Falls
paras: Rainbow Falls is a good short hike if you want a waterfall and forest without committing to the full Rainbow Lake hike. The trail follows a forested route to a pretty waterfall viewpoint.
The hike is about 2 to 3 km round trip, with around 100 m of elevation gain, and usually takes 45 minutes to 1.5 hours. It is easy to moderate, with roots, rocks, and some uphill sections.
This is a good choice for a half-day or rainy-day forest walk.
items.note: The trail can be wet and slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip.

items.name: Brandywine Falls Trail
paras: Brandywine Falls is one of the easiest waterfall walks near Whistler. It is located south of Whistler along the Sea to Sky Highway and makes a great stop on the drive to or from town.
The walk to the viewpoint is short, usually about 1 km round trip, with minimal elevation gain, and takes about 20 to 30 minutes. The viewpoint overlooks a dramatic waterfall dropping into a canyon.
Best for: Families, road trips, waterfall photos, easy walks.
items.note: Stay behind barriers and use marked trails. The canyon edges are dangerous.

items.name: Ancient Cedars Trail
items.alt: A hiker passing giant cedars
paras: Ancient Cedars Trail is a good forest hike for people who want to see big old trees without doing a major mountain climb. The trail leads through peaceful forest to large cedar trees, giving visitors a quieter side of Whistler.
The hike is about 5 km round trip, with around 175 m of elevation gain, and usually takes 1.5 to 2.5 hours. It is easy to moderate, depending on trail conditions and your hiking pace.
This is a nice option on a warm day because much of the route is shaded.
items.note: The access road can be rough or seasonal, so check conditions before going.

items.name: Cheakamus Lake Trail
items.alt: A glassy lake with snow peaks behind
paras: Cheakamus Lake is one of the best moderate lake hikes near Whistler. The trail follows forest and river scenery before reaching a beautiful turquoise lake surrounded by mountains.

The hike to the lake is about 14 km round trip if you go to the main lake area and return, with around 400 m of elevation gain, and usually takes 4 to 5 hours. The trail is easier than many alpine hikes because the climb is more gradual, but it is still a longer outing.
This is a great choice if you want a full nature experience without the steep effort of Rainbow Lake, Garibaldi Lake, or Wedgemount Lake.
items.note: Cheakamus Lake is in Garibaldi Provincial Park, so check current access, parking, and pass requirements before going.

items.name: Crater Rim and Logger’s Lake
paras: Crater Rim and Logger’s Lake offer a more local-feeling hike in the Cheakamus area. The route climbs through forest to viewpoints over Logger’s Lake, which sits in an old volcanic crater.
The hike is about 4 to 5 km, with roughly 200 m of elevation gain, and usually takes 1.5 to 2.5 hours. It is moderate because the trail has rocky sections, roots, and short climbs.
This is a good hike if you want something shorter than Cheakamus Lake but more active than Train Wreck.
items.note: Trails in this area can connect with other routes, so use a map or offline trail app.

items.name: Blackcomb Alpine Trails
paras: Blackcomb Mountain has several alpine hiking options, ranging from short scenic walks to harder loops. These trails are accessed by gondola and are great for visitors who want mountain scenery, wildflowers, glaciers, and alpine views without starting from the valley floor.

Distances and difficulty vary. Some short alpine walks may take 30 minutes to 1 hour, while longer routes can take 2 to 4 hours or more. Elevation gain also depends on the trail, but even easier alpine walks can feel more tiring because of uneven ground and high-mountain conditions.
Best for: Alpine meadows, mountain views, families, photography, gondola-accessed hiking.
items.note: Check lift hours and trail status before going. Alpine trails may open later in the season because of snow.

items.name: Rainbow Lake
paras: Rainbow Lake is one of Whistler’s classic hard day hikes. It is long, steady, and rewarding, with forest, creek crossings, waterfalls, mountain views, and a beautiful lake at the end.
The hike is about 16 km round trip, with around 850 m of elevation gain, and usually takes 6 to 8 hours. It is a hard hike because of the distance and steady climb.
This is a strong choice for fit hikers who want a full-day trail close to Whistler.
items.note: Swimming is not allowed in Rainbow Lake because it is part of Whistler’s drinking water supply. Dogs are also not allowed on this trail.

items.name: High Note Trail
paras: High Note Trail is one of the best alpine hikes in Whistler. It starts from the top of Whistler Mountain and gives huge views over Cheakamus Lake, Black Tusk, Garibaldi Provincial Park, alpine meadows, rocky slopes, and surrounding peaks.

The full High Note Trail is about 9 to 10 km, with about 430 m of elevation change, and usually takes 3 to 4.5 hours. It is moderate to hard because it is in alpine terrain, with uneven ground, exposure, and changing weather.
This is one of the best hikes for visitors who want big mountain views without hiking all the way up from the valley.
items.note: You need lift access, and the trail is only available when mountain operations and trail conditions allow. Bring layers because the alpine can be much cooler than the village.

items.name: Decker Loop
paras: Decker Loop is one of the best advanced hikes on Blackcomb Mountain. It connects with the Overlord Trail and gives views of glaciers, alpine lakes, rugged peaks, and high mountain terrain.

The loop from the Top of the World area to the Roundhouse Lodge area usually takes about 3 to 4 hours, depending on pace and conditions. It is a hard alpine route, with rocky terrain and more serious mountain conditions than a simple sightseeing walk.
This is a good choice for hikers who want a bigger alpine experience after riding up the mountain.
items.note: This trail enters serious alpine terrain. Check lift schedules, weather, and trail status before starting.

items.name: Garibaldi Lake
paras: Garibaldi Lake is one of the most famous hikes in the Sea to Sky area. It is south of Whistler, but many Whistler visitors include it as a big hiking day.

The hike is about 18 km round trip, with around 820 m of elevation gain, and usually takes 5 to 7+ hours. The trail climbs steadily through forest before reaching a bright blue glacier-fed lake surrounded by mountains.
This is a hard full-day hike, but the lake is one of the most beautiful hiking rewards near Whistler.
items.note: Garibaldi Provincial Park may require a free day-use pass during busy periods. Check BC Parks rules before going.

items.name: Singing Pass Trail
paras: Singing Pass is a long and demanding route that connects the Whistler Village area with the alpine around Garibaldi Provincial Park. It is often used by experienced hikers heading toward Russet Lake, Musical Bumps, or longer backcountry routes.
The trail is about 22 km one way if hiking from the village toward the alpine, with significant elevation gain. Many people use it as part of a longer backcountry plan rather than a casual day hike.
This is not a beginner hike. It is best for prepared hikers who understand route planning, weather, distance, and backcountry travel.
items.note: Plan carefully. Check current trail conditions, snow, daylight, and whether lift-assisted route options are available.

items.name: Wedgemount Lake
items.alt: A turquoise lake below bare mountains
paras: Wedgemount Lake is one of the hardest popular hikes near Whistler. It is steep, rocky, and demanding, but the reward is dramatic: a bright alpine lake below glacier-covered peaks.
The hike is about 12 to 14 km round trip, with around 1,200 m of elevation gain, and usually takes 6 to 8+ hours. It is very hard because the climb is steep almost the whole way.
This hike is best for strong, prepared hikers with good footwear, enough water, layers, and mountain experience.
items.note: This is much harder than the distance suggests. Do not choose it as your first Whistler hike.

faqs.q: What is the best hike in Whistler?
a: For easy hiking, Lost Lake and Train Wreck are two of the best choices. For alpine views, High Note Trail is one of the best hikes in Whistler. For a hard full-day lake hike, Garibaldi Lake, Rainbow Lake, and Wedgemount Lake are popular choices.

faqs.q: What is the easiest hike in Whistler?
a: Lost Lake Loop, the Valley Trail, Train Wreck, Rainbow Falls, and Brandywine Falls are some of the easiest hikes and walks in Whistler.

faqs.q: What is the best alpine hike in Whistler?
a: High Note Trail is one of the best alpine hikes in Whistler because it offers views of Cheakamus Lake, Black Tusk, Garibaldi Provincial Park, and surrounding peaks. Blackcomb’s Decker Loop is another strong alpine option for more experienced hikers.

faqs.q: Can beginners hike in Whistler?
a: Yes. Beginners can start with Lost Lake, the Valley Trail, Train Wreck, Rainbow Falls, Brandywine Falls, or short gondola-accessed alpine walks.

faqs.q: Is Wedgemount Lake hard?
a: Yes. Wedgemount Lake is very hard. It has a steep climb, rough terrain, and major elevation gain. It is best for strong, prepared hikers.

faqs.q: Do you need a pass to hike in Whistler?
a: Some nearby hikes in Garibaldi Provincial Park may require free day-use passes during busy periods. Lift-access alpine hikes require sightseeing or lift access. Always check current rules before going.

faqs.q: Can you hike in Whistler in winter?
a: Some lower trails and the Valley Trail can be used in winter, but many hiking trails are covered in snow. Lost Lake becomes a Nordic skiing and snowshoeing area, and alpine hiking routes are usually not summer hiking trails in winter.

faqs.q: What should I hike if I only have one day in Whistler?
a: For an easy day, choose Lost Lake, Train Wreck, or the Valley Trail. For alpine views, ride the gondola and hike High Note or shorter alpine trails if open. For a hard full-day hike, choose Garibaldi Lake, Rainbow Lake, or Wedgemount Lake if conditions are safe.

Whistler is one of the best hiking destinations in British Columbia because it offers so many trail types in one place. You can take an easy village walk, hike through old forest, cross a suspension bridge, follow a river to a turquoise lake, or ride a gondola into the alpine.

For first-time visitors, Lost Lake, Train Wreck, and High Note Trail are great starting points. For families, choose Lost Lake, the Valley Trail, Rainbow Falls, or Brandywine Falls. For stronger hikers, Rainbow Lake, Garibaldi Lake, Decker Loop, and Wedgemount Lake offer bigger adventure.

faqs.q: Is Whistler good for hiking in summer?
a: Yes. Summer is one of the best times to hike in Whistler. Lower trails open earlier, while alpine trails are best once snow has melted and lifts are operating.

items.name: Fitzsimmons Zone
paras: The Fitzsimmons Zone is the original and most famous part of the bike park. It is close to Whistler Village and is where many riders start. This zone has beginner-friendly progression trails, classic flow trails, technical trails, and some of the most famous lines in the park.
It is a good place to build confidence, repeat laps, and learn how the bike park works.
Best for: First bike park experience, progression, classic Whistler trails, quick laps from the village.

items.name: Creekside Zone
paras: The Creekside Zone gives riders another access point and a different style of terrain. It is popular with riders who want longer descents, a little more space, and a different base area from the main village.
This zone is better for riders who already feel comfortable on mountain bike trails.
Best for: Intermediate riders, longer laps, quieter access, riders staying near Creekside.

items.name: Garbanzo Zone
paras: Garbanzo takes riders higher up the mountain. Trails here are longer, rougher, and more demanding than the lower mountain. Riders should be comfortable with sustained downhill riding, braking, body position, and fatigue.
Best for: Intermediate to advanced riders, longer descents, more physical riding.

items.name: Peak Zone and Top of the World
paras: The Peak Zone gives riders a high-alpine experience with big mountain views. Top of the World is one of Whistler’s most iconic alpine bike trails, but it is not for beginners. The terrain is exposed, rocky, and more serious than lower park trails.
Best for: Advanced and expert riders, alpine views, bucket-list Whistler biking.
Yes, beginners can bike in Whistler, but they should choose the right type of riding.
items.note: Do not judge bike park trails by ski-run colors alone. A green downhill bike trail can still feel harder than a normal paved or gravel ride.

items.name: The Valley Trail: Easy Biking in Whistler
items.alt: Cyclists on the Valley Trail beside the lake
paras: The Valley Trail is one of the best ways to bike in Whistler if you are not looking for downhill riding. It is a paved, car-free trail network that connects Whistler Village with lakes, parks, neighborhoods, viewpoints, and picnic areas.
This is the best choice for families, casual riders, couples, and visitors who want to explore Whistler without driving.
You can use the Valley Trail to bike to:
items.note: The Valley Trail is shared by walkers, runners, cyclists, children, and dogs. Ride slowly in busy areas and use your bell when passing.

items.name: Lost Lake Biking
items.alt: A forested lake with a small island
paras: Lost Lake is one of the easiest places to enjoy biking close to Whistler Village. The area has paved access through the Valley Trail, plus forest trails nearby for riders who want a little more adventure.
Casual riders can bike to the lake for swimming, a picnic, or a short loop. More confident riders can explore nearby cross-country trails.
Best for: Families, beginner riders, lake rides, easy forest biking, short trips from the village.
items.note: Book rentals and lessons early during summer weekends, holidays, and bike events.

items.name: Crankworx Whistler
paras: Crankworx Whistler is the biggest mountain biking event in Whistler and one of the most important bike festivals in the world. It is usually held in summer, most often in July or August.
The event brings together professional riders, amateur riders, bike fans, brands, demos, races, Kidsworx events, and a high-energy village atmosphere. It is not just one race.

Crankworx includes several styles of mountain bike competition, such as slopestyle, downhill, dual slalom, pump track, enduro, and other gravity-focused events. These events show different sides of mountain biking: big tricks, technical downhill speed, head-to-head racing, tight cornering, stamina, and bike handling.
items.note: Whistler gets very busy during Crankworx. Book lodging, bike rentals, restaurants, and activities early. Some trails, village areas, and bike park zones may also be affected by events, so check the current schedule before planning your riding days.

items.name: RBC GranFondo Whistler
paras: RBC GranFondo Whistler is a major road cycling event from Vancouver to Whistler along the Sea to Sky Highway. It is usually held in September, making it a late-summer or early-fall cycling event.

This is a different kind of biking event from Crankworx. Instead of downhill mountain biking, GranFondo focuses on endurance road cycling, scenic highway riding, and a big finish in Whistler. Riders travel about 122 km from Vancouver to Whistler, following the Sea to Sky corridor in a large organized cycling event.
It is relevant for serious road cyclists, endurance riders, spectators, and visitors who want to see a major cycling event in the region.
items.note: The event can affect road travel and traffic between Vancouver and Whistler. Plan ahead if you are driving on event day, especially along the Sea to Sky Highway.

items.name: UCI Mountain Bike World Cup Downhill
paras: Whistler will host the UCI Mountain Bike World Cup Downhill for the first time in 2026. It is scheduled for September 25 to 27, 2026, making it a fall mountain biking event.

This is not a long-running annual Whistler event like Crankworx. Instead, 2026 marks the event’s Whistler debut, bringing an official UCI World Cup downhill race to one of the most famous mountain biking destinations in the world.

The event focuses on downhill racing, where elite riders race one at a time down a steep, technical course, with the fastest time winning. The Whistler stop is expected to take place in the Creekside area of Whistler Mountain Bike Park.
items.note: Because this is a major first-time World Cup event for Whistler, expect strong interest from mountain bike fans. Event dates, trail access, bike park operations, village crowds, and travel plans may affect the normal riding experience, so check the current event schedule before booking or planning your riding days.

faqs.q: What is Whistler known for in biking?
a: Whistler is best known for Whistler Mountain Bike Park, lift-accessed downhill riding, Crankworx Whistler, cross-country trails, the Valley Trail, and its strong summer bike culture.

faqs.q: Is Whistler good for non-mountain bikers?
a: Yes. Whistler is excellent even if you are not a mountain biker. The Valley Trail, lake rides, e-bike tours, Lost Lake, and casual rentals make biking accessible for visitors who just want an easy outdoor activity.

You do not need to ride the bike park to enjoy biking in Whistler. For many travelers, the best biking day is a simple ride from the village to Lost Lake or Alta Lake, with a picnic or swim along the way.

faqs.q: Is Whistler Bike Park good for beginners?
a: Yes, but beginners should approach it carefully. Whistler Bike Park has beginner trails, lessons, and progression routes, but it is still a downhill mountain bike park. That means steeper terrain, higher speeds, berms, braking bumps, and trail features.
The best beginner plan is to rent proper gear, take a lesson, start on green trails, and avoid comparing yourself to experienced riders.

faqs.q: Do you need a special bike for Whistler Bike Park?
a: Yes. For the bike park, use a downhill or enduro mountain bike with proper suspension and brakes. A casual bike, cruiser bike, or basic hybrid bike is not suitable for downhill park trails.

faqs.q: Is Whistler Bike Park only for experts?
a: No. Whistler Bike Park has trails for different levels, including beginner and intermediate routes. However, first-time riders should take a lesson and start slowly.

faqs.q: What is the easiest biking in Whistler?
a: The Valley Trail is the easiest biking option in Whistler. It is paved, scenic, and connects the village with lakes, parks, and neighborhoods.

faqs.q: What is the best biking event in Whistler?
a: Crankworx Whistler is the top biking event for mountain bike fans. RBC GranFondo Whistler is the major event for road cyclists.

faqs.q: When is Crankworx Whistler?
a: Crankworx Whistler is usually held in summer. For 2026, it is scheduled for July 24 to August 2.

faqs.q: When is the best time to bike in Whistler?
a: The best biking season is usually summer, especially June through September. Fall can also be excellent, depending on weather, trail conditions, and lift operations.

faqs.q: Can you e-bike in Whistler?
a: Yes. E-bikes are available in Whistler and are popular for scenic rides, the Valley Trail, and guided tours. Check local rules because not all trails allow all types of e-bikes.

faqs.q: Is biking in Whistler expensive?
a: It can be, especially if you rent a downhill bike, buy bike park tickets, book lessons, or visit during major events. Casual Valley Trail biking can be more affordable, especially if you bring your own bike or rent a simple cruiser.
Biking is one of the best ways to experience Whistler in summer. The bike park gives Whistler its world-famous downhill reputation, but the destination is much more than expert mountain biking.

Beginners can cruise the Valley Trail, families can ride to Lost Lake, casual visitors can rent e-bikes, cross-country riders can explore forest trails, and experienced riders can spend days in the bike park.

faqs.q: Is Whistler worth visiting in summer if you do not bike?
a: Yes. Whistler is worth visiting in summer even if you do not mountain bike. You can ride the Peak 2 Peak Gondola, hike, swim, paddle, walk the Valley Trail, visit museums, relax at the spa, enjoy lake parks, go ziplining, take photos, eat out, or simply enjoy the village.

faqs.q: Can beginners mountain bike in Whistler?
a: Yes, but beginners should take a lesson or start with easier valley trails before trying the bike park. The Whistler Bike Park has beginner options, but it is still a real downhill biking environment.

subs.h: Whistler Blackcomb: The Main Ski Area

items.name: Safety Tips for Whistler Blackcomb
items.alt: Whistler and Blackcomb ski runs above the village at dusk
paras: Whistler Blackcomb is a resort, but it is still a mountain environment. Weather, visibility, snow conditions, crowds, and fatigue all affect safety.
Stay in control at all times. You should be able to stop or avoid people and objects.
Give people downhill of you the right of way. It is your responsibility to avoid them.
items.note: Never ski trees alone. Tree wells can be dangerous, especially after heavy snowfall.

items.name: Ski or Snowboard at Whistler Blackcomb
items.alt: Four skiers on a ridge with the Black Tusk behind
paras: Skiing and snowboarding are the main reasons many people visit Whistler in winter. Whistler Blackcomb has two mountains, a large lift system, wide terrain, ski schools, rentals, on-mountain dining, and a lively village at the base.

There are runs for many ability levels, from beginner-friendly areas to advanced bowls, glades, and steep terrain. If you are new to skiing or snowboarding, lessons are a smart choice. They help you learn safely and make the mountain less overwhelming.
Best for: Skiing, snowboarding, winter vacations, families, lessons, après-ski.
items.note: Book lift tickets, lessons, rentals, and accommodation early. Winter holidays and weekends can be very busy.

items.name: Ride the Peak 2 Peak Gondola
items.alt: A child in a red gondola cabin with skis, mountains behind
paras: The Peak 2 Peak Gondola is one of Whistler’s most famous attractions in both winter and summer. In winter, it connects Whistler and Blackcomb Mountains and gives big views over snowy forests, ski runs, mountain peaks, and the valley below.
You do not need to be a skier to enjoy it. Sightseeing visitors can ride up for views, photos, mountain restaurants, and the feeling of being high in the alpine.
Best for: First-time visitors, non-skiers, views, photography, families.
items.note: Dress warmly. It can be much colder and windier on the mountain than in the village.

items.name: Explore Whistler Village
items.alt: Whistler Village in the evening, lit and snowy
paras: Whistler Village is one of the best parts of a winter trip. It is walkable, lively, and full of restaurants, shops, cafes, bars, hotels, galleries, and ski rental stores.
In the morning, the village feels energetic as skiers head to the lifts. In the afternoon, it fills with après-ski crowds. At night, lights, snow, and mountain views make it feel cozy and festive.
Best for: Food, shopping, après-ski, nightlife, easy walking, non-skiers.
items.note: Stay near the village if you want the easiest access to restaurants, lift bases, tours, and shops without driving.

items.name: Go Snowshoeing
items.alt: Snowshoers on a forest trail
paras: Snowshoeing is one of the best winter activities in Whistler for non-skiers. It lets you walk through snowy forest trails without needing downhill ski skills.

You can snowshoe on maintained trails, book a guided snowshoe tour, or combine it with a quiet winter nature day. It is slower than skiing, but that is part of the appeal. You get time to enjoy the snow, trees, and mountain silence.
Best for: Non-skiers, families, winter walks, nature, quiet snow days.
items.note: Wear warm waterproof boots, layers, gloves, and a hat. Trails may require passes or rentals depending on where you go.

items.name: Try Tubing
items.alt: Two people sliding on a snow tube
paras: Tubing is one of the easiest snow activities in Whistler. You do not need ski or snowboard experience. You sit in an inflatable tube and slide down a groomed snow lane.
It is a fun option for families, groups, and visitors who want a simple winter activity without lessons or special skills.
Best for: Families, kids, groups, non-skiers, easy snow fun.
items.note: Dress warmly and wear waterproof clothing. Check height, age, and operating rules before going.

items.name: Cross-Country Ski at Lost Lake
items.alt: A cross-country skier in low sun
paras: Lost Lake is popular in summer, but in winter it becomes a Nordic skiing and snowshoeing area. It is close to the village and offers a quieter snow experience than the downhill ski slopes.
Cross-country skiing is a good choice if you want exercise, winter scenery, and a slower pace. It can be peaceful, but it still gives you a great workout.
Best for: Fitness, peaceful winter trails, non-downhill skiers, families with older kids.
items.note: Trail access, rentals, and passes may be required. Check current Lost Lake winter operations before going.

items.name: Relax at Scandinave Spa
items.alt: Three people in an outdoor hot pool in the snow
paras: Scandinave Spa is one of Whistler’s best winter wellness experiences. It is known for outdoor hot baths, cold plunges, steam rooms, saunas, quiet spaces, and a forest setting.
Winter makes the spa feel extra special. Sitting in warm water while snow surrounds the pools is one of the most relaxing ways to enjoy Whistler.
Best for: Couples, wellness, recovery after skiing, quiet time, adults.
items.note: The spa is quiet and phone-free. Book ahead because it is very popular in winter.

items.name: Visit the Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre
items.alt: Carved cedar drums at the Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre
paras: The Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre is one of the most meaningful places to visit in Whistler. It shares the living cultures, stories, art, and traditions of the Squamish Nation and Lil’wat Nation.
This is a great winter activity when you want a break from the cold, skiing, or busy village crowds. It also helps visitors understand the land beyond the resort experience.
Best for: Culture, Indigenous learning, families, indoor activity, rest days.
items.note: Give yourself enough time to explore the exhibits and join a guided experience if available.

items.name: Visit the Audain Art Museum
items.alt: The snowy approach to the Audain Art Museum
paras: The Audain Art Museum is a strong indoor activity for winter. It is close to Whistler Village and features art from British Columbia, including important Indigenous art and works by major regional artists.
It is a good option for snowy, rainy, very cold, or low-energy days when you still want to do something meaningful.
Best for: Art, culture, rainy days, rest days, couples, families with older kids.
items.note: Pair it with a village lunch, coffee stop, or visit to the Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre.

items.name: Try Snowmobiling
items.alt: Snowmobiles crossing a snowy forest trail
paras: Snowmobiling is one of Whistler’s classic winter adventure tours. Guided trips take you through snowy forest roads, mountain terrain, and scenic winter areas.
It is a good activity if you want something faster and more adventurous than snowshoeing, but you do not want to ski or snowboard.
Best for: Adventure travelers, groups, couples, winter scenery, guided tours.
items.note: Check age, driver’s license, clothing, and safety requirements before booking. Tours can sell out during peak winter dates.

items.name: Go Winter Ziplining
paras: Ziplining is not only a summer activity. In winter, zipline tours can give you a different view of Whistler’s snowy forests, creeks, and mountain scenery.
It is a fun option if you want a guided activity with a bit of thrill, but without needing ski skills.
Best for: Groups, couples, families with older kids, thrill seekers, non-skiers.
items.note: Dress warmly because you may be standing outside between ziplines. Gloves, warm socks, and layers are important.

items.name: Enjoy Après-Ski and Dining
items.alt: People around an outdoor fire after skiing
paras: Après-ski is a major part of winter in Whistler. After a day on the mountain, people gather in the village for drinks, food, music, patios with heaters, casual pubs, and cozy restaurants.
You can enjoy après-ski even if you did not ski. The village has everything from coffee and bakeries to casual meals, fine dining, cocktail bars, family restaurants, and late-night spots.
Best for: Food, drinks, nightlife, groups, couples, relaxed evenings.
items.note: Popular restaurants and après spots can be busy. Make reservations for dinner, especially on weekends and holidays.

items.name: Go Ice Skating
items.alt: Two people skating hand in hand on a frozen lake
paras: Ice skating is a fun, classic winter activity for families, couples, and non-skiers. Whistler usually offers seasonal outdoor skating in the village area, depending on weather and operations.
It is a good option if you want something easy and festive without leaving town.
Best for: Families, couples, kids, winter atmosphere, easy activity.
items.note: Check current rink location, hours, and rental information before going.

faqs.q: What is Whistler best known for in winter?
a: Whistler is best known for Whistler Blackcomb, skiing, snowboarding, the Peak 2 Peak Gondola, après-ski, alpine bowls, long runs, and its walkable winter village.

faqs.q: Is Whistler Blackcomb one ski resort or two?
a: Whistler Blackcomb is one resort made up of two mountains: Whistler Mountain and Blackcomb Mountain. They are connected by the Peak 2 Peak Gondola.

faqs.q: Which is better, Whistler Mountain or Blackcomb Mountain?
a: Both are excellent. Whistler Mountain is often a classic choice for first-time visitors and village access. Blackcomb is also large and varied, with strong intermediate and advanced terrain. Many visitors try both.

faqs.q: Is Whistler better for skiers or snowboarders?
a: Whistler is excellent for both skiers and snowboarders. Skiers may enjoy the long groomers, alpine bowls, moguls, and steep terrain. Snowboarders often enjoy the wide runs, terrain parks, powder, and tree riding.

The main challenge for snowboarders can be flat sections and traverses, especially when moving around the mountain. Beginners on snowboards should take lessons to learn how to manage speed, edges, and lift exits.

faqs.q: Is Whistler good for advanced skiers and snowboarders?
a: Yes. Advanced riders have a lot to explore at Whistler Blackcomb, including alpine bowls, steep marked runs, tree skiing, powder areas, moguls, and glacier terrain.
The key is to follow current signs, closures, and patrol guidance. Whistler’s advanced terrain can change quickly with weather and visibility.

faqs.q: When is the best time to ski in Whistler?
a: The best time for a ski-focused trip is usually January to March. December is festive but busy, and April can offer spring skiing with more variable conditions.

faqs.q: Do you need to book lift tickets in advance?
a: Booking lift tickets in advance is recommended, especially during holidays, weekends, and peak ski dates. It can also help you avoid last-minute stress.

faqs.q: Can non-skiers go up the mountain?
a: Yes. Non-skiers can ride the Peak 2 Peak Gondola for sightseeing when sightseeing access is operating. They can also enjoy the village, tubing, snowshoeing, spas, museums, and dining.

faqs.q: Is Whistler expensive for skiing?
a: Yes, Whistler can be expensive. Lift tickets, rentals, lessons, hotels, restaurants, and parking can add up. Book early, visit midweek, avoid peak holidays, and consider package deals if you want to save.

Skiing and snowboarding in Whistler is one of the classic winter experiences in British Columbia. Whistler Blackcomb is huge, scenic, and full of variety, with terrain for beginners, families, intermediates, advanced riders, and experts.

For a first trip, keep your plan simple. Book lessons if you are new, choose one mountain for your first day, check the trail map, and do not rush to ski everything. For stronger riders, use several days to explore Whistler Mountain, Blackcomb Mountain, alpine bowls, trees, groomers, and terrain parks.

faqs.q: What can you do in Whistler in winter besides skiing?
a: You can snowshoe, cross-country ski, ride the Peak 2 Peak Gondola, visit the village, relax at Scandinave Spa, visit museums, go shopping, enjoy après-ski, or take a snowmobile tour.

faqs.q: What is Whistler known for in winter?
a: Whistler is known for skiing, snowboarding, Whistler Blackcomb, Peak 2 Peak Gondola, après-ski, winter village atmosphere, snowshoeing, tubing, spas, and winter adventure tours.

faqs.q: Is Whistler expensive in winter?
a: Yes, Whistler can be expensive in winter. Hotels, lift tickets, rentals, lessons, tours, restaurants, and parking can add up quickly. Prices are usually highest during holidays, weekends, and peak ski dates.
You can save money by visiting midweek, avoiding Christmas and New Year, booking early, staying outside the village, choosing non-ski activities, cooking some meals, or planning a shorter trip.

faqs.q: Is Whistler good for beginners in winter?
a: Yes. Beginners can take ski or snowboard lessons, try tubing, go snowshoeing, ride the gondola, walk the village, or do easy guided winter activities.

faqs.q: Is Whistler good for families in winter?
a: Yes. Whistler is very family-friendly in winter. Families can ski, snowboard, take lessons, go tubing, ice skate, snowshoe, enjoy hot chocolate stops, walk the village, and visit indoor attractions.

faqs.q: Can non-skiers ride the Peak 2 Peak Gondola?
a: Yes. Non-skiers can ride the Peak 2 Peak Gondola for winter sightseeing when sightseeing access is operating. Check current lift and ticket details before going.

faqs.q: Do you need a car in Whistler in winter?
a: Not always. If you stay near Whistler Village, many restaurants, shops, lifts, rentals, and tour meeting points are walkable. A car is helpful for side trips, but winter driving requires more planning.

faqs.q: Is it hard to drive to Whistler in winter?
a: The Sea to Sky Highway is scenic but can have winter driving conditions, including rain, snow, ice, and heavy traffic. Check road reports before driving a nd make sure your vehicle meets winter tire or chain requirements.

faqs.q: How many days do you need in Whistler in winter?
a: One day is enough for a quick village and gondola visit, but two to four days is better if you want to ski, snowboard, snowshoe, enjoy the spa, try winter tours, and have time to relax.
Winter in Whistler is the classic Whistler experience: snowy mountains, busy lifts, cozy village nights, après-ski, winter tours, and beautiful views in every direction.

If you ski or snowboard, Whistler Blackcomb is the main event. If you do not ski, you can still have a full winter trip with the Peak 2 Peak Gondola, snowshoeing, tubing, spa time, museums, village walks, shopping, dining, and guided tours.

items.name: Ride the Peak 2 Peak Gondola
items.alt: A child in a red gondola cabin with skis, mountains behind
paras: The Peak 2 Peak Gondola is one of Whistler’s most famous attractions. It connects Whistler Mountain and Blackcomb Mountain, giving visitors a huge alpine sightseeing experience without needing to ski or hike.

The ride gives you views of forests, valleys, peaks, snowfields, and Whistler Village below. In summer, a sightseeing ticket can also give access to alpine trails, mountain viewpoints, and the Whistler Peak Suspension Bridge when open. In winter, it is part of the mountain experience for skiers and sightseeing visitors.
Mountain temperatures are often 5 to 10°C cooler than the village, so dress in layers even on warm days.
items.note: Hours and access change by season, so check the current schedule before going. Wear sturdy shoes if you plan to walk or hike in the alpine.

items.name: Ski or Snowboard at Whistler Blackcomb
items.alt: Four skiers on a ridge with the Black Tusk behind
paras: Whistler Blackcomb is the biggest reason many people visit Whistler in winter. It is known as North America’s largest ski resort, with two mountains, wide terrain, ski schools, rentals, on-mountain dining, and a lively village at the base.
There are runs for different levels, from beginner-friendly slopes to advanced bowls and steeps. Even if you are new to skiing or snowboarding, lessons make it easier to enjoy the mountain safely.
Best for:Skiing, snowboarding, winter vacations, families, lessons, après-ski
items.note: Winter is a busy season. Book lodging, lift tickets, rentals, and lessons early, especially around holidays and weekends.

items.name: Explore Whistler Village
items.alt: Whistler Village in the evening, lit and snowy
paras: Whistler Village is the heart of the resort. It is walkable, lively, and easy to enjoy without a car. You can wander between shops, restaurants, cafes, bars, hotels, galleries, gear stores, and lift bases.
In winter, the village feels cozy and festive. In summer, patios, bikes, outdoor events, and mountain views make it a great place to spend time between activities.
Whistler Village is good for:
items.note: If you are visiting for the first time, stay near the village if you want the easiest access to restaurants, shops, lifts, and tours.

items.name: Visit Lost Lake
items.alt: A forested lake with a small island
paras: Lost Lake is one of the best easy nature spots in Whistler. It is close to the village but feels peaceful and forested.

In summer, visitors come here to swim, picnic, walk, bike, paddle, and relax by the water. In winter, the area becomes a place for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, with a large network of Nordic trails.
Winter cross-country skiing
items.note: It can get busy in summer. Go earlier in the day if you want a quieter lake visit.

items.name: Go Mountain Biking
paras: Whistler is one of the world’s best-known mountain biking destinations. The Whistler Mountain Bike Park is famous for lift-access downhill biking, flow trails, jump lines, technical terrain, and bike culture.
If you are not ready for downhill riding, there are also easier valley trails and scenic bike paths around town. You can rent bikes, take lessons, or choose guided rides.
Mountain biking in Whistler is best for:
items.note: The bike park can be intense for beginners. Start with lessons or easier trails if you are new.

items.name: Hike in the Alpine
paras: Whistler is a great hiking destination in summer and early fall. The alpine trails are especially beautiful because you can reach high mountain areas by gondola.

Depending on the season and lift access, you may find trails with wildflowers, viewpoints, lakes, ridgelines, and mountain scenery. Summer sightseeing can include access to over 50 km of hiking, running, and interpretive walking trails.
Good hiking options include:
items.note: Alpine weather can change quickly. Bring layers, water, sun protection, and proper footwear.

items.name: Walk or Bike the Valley Trail
items.alt: Cyclists on the Valley Trail beside the lake
paras: The Valley Trail is one of the easiest ways to explore Whistler. It is a paved path system that connects neighborhoods, lakes, parks, viewpoints, and Whistler Village.
You can walk, bike, run, or cruise between places without needing to drive. This is one of the best family-friendly activities in Whistler, especially in summer.
The Valley Trail is good for:
items.note: Rent a bike if you want to cover more ground. The path is shared, so stay aware of walkers, cyclists, and children.

items.name: Visit the Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre
items.alt: Carved cedar drums at the Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre
paras: The Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre is one of the most meaningful places to visit in Whistler. It shares the living cultures, stories, art, and traditions of the Squamish Nation and Lil’wat Nation.
This is a great stop if you want to understand the land beyond the resort experience. It is also a good rainy-day activity and a strong choice for families.
Best for:Culture, Indigenous learning, art, history, rainy days, families
items.note: Give yourself enough time to explore the exhibits and consider joining a guided experience if available.

items.name: Relax at Scandinave Spa
items.alt: Three people in an outdoor hot pool in the snow
paras: Scandinave Spa is one of Whistler’s most popular wellness experiences. It is known for outdoor hot baths, cold plunges, steam rooms, saunas, quiet spaces, and a peaceful forest setting.
This is a great choice after skiing, hiking, biking, or a long travel day.
Best for:Couples, relaxation, wellness, rainy days, recovery after outdoor activities
items.note: The spa is quiet and phone-free, so it is best for adults and travelers looking for calm rather than a social pool experience.

items.name: Visit the Audain Art Museum
items.alt: The snowy approach to the Audain Art Museum
paras: The Audain Art Museum is a strong cultural stop in Whistler. It features art from British Columbia, including important Indigenous art and works by major regional artists.
It is a good choice when the weather is rainy, when you want a slower day, or when you want a break from outdoor activities.
Best for:Art, culture, rainy days, quiet afternoons, couples, families with older kids
items.note: Pair it with the Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre for a culture-focused Whistler day.

items.name: Try Ziplining or Adventure Tours
paras: Whistler has many adventure tours that are easy to book, especially in summer. Ziplining is one of the most popular choices, but you may also find ATV tours, rafting, bungee jumping, off-road tours, and snowmobile trips depending on the season.
Adventure tours are good if you want excitement but do not have your own gear.
Best for:Groups, families with older kids, thrill seekers, first-time visitors, guided adventure
items.note: Check age, height, weight, and weather rules before booking.

items.name: Paddle or Relax at Whistler Lakes
paras: Whistler has several lakes that are great in summer. Lost Lake, Alta Lake, Green Lake, and Nita Lake are all popular for different reasons.
You can swim, paddleboard, canoe, kayak, picnic, walk, bike, or just relax by the water.
Whistler lakes are good for:
items.note: Lake water can still be cold early in the season. Bring layers and check rental options before going.

items.name: Go Snowshoeing or Cross-Country Skiing
items.alt: A cross-country skier in low sun
paras: Whistler is not only for downhill skiing. If you want a quieter winter activity, try snowshoeing or cross-country skiing.
Lost Lake is one of the most convenient areas for Nordic skiing and snowshoeing. It feels peaceful and forested, even though it is close to the village.
Best for:Winter nature, families, non-skiers, peaceful snow days, exercise
items.note: Rentals and trail passes may be needed depending on where you go. Check current trail conditions before heading out.

items.name: Enjoy Après-Ski and Dining
items.alt: People around an outdoor fire after skiing
paras: Whistler is famous for après-ski, restaurants, patios, bars, and mountain-town dining. After skiing, biking, hiking, or sightseeing, the village has plenty of places to eat and relax.
You can find everything from casual pubs and pizza to fine dining, cafes, bakeries, cocktail bars, sushi, and family-friendly restaurants.
Whistler dining is good for:
items.note: Make reservations for popular dinner spots, especially in winter, summer, and on weekends.

items.name: Drive the Sea to Sky Highway
paras: Getting to Whistler is part of the experience. The Sea to Sky Highway between Vancouver and Whistler is one of British Columbia’s most scenic drives.
On the way, you can stop at viewpoints, waterfalls, Squamish, the Sea to Sky Gondola, Shannon Falls, Brandywine Falls, or other short nature stops.
Peak 2 Peak Gondola, Whistler Village, Lost Lake, Valley Trail
items.note: In winter, check road conditions and make sure your vehicle is properly equipped for mountain travel.

items.name: Try Ziplining, ATV Tours, or Rafting
paras: Whistler has many bookable adventure tours. Depending on the season, you may find ziplining, ATV tours, rafting, snowmobiling, snowshoeing, and other guided activities.

items.name: Spend the Day at Lost Lake
items.alt: A forested lake with a small island
paras: Lost Lake is one of the easiest and most popular summer spots in Whistler. It is close to the village and has a beach, swimming areas, walking trails, biking trails, and picnic spots.

You can walk or bike there from Whistler Village, spend a few hours by the water, or make it part of a longer Valley Trail route. It is a good option for families, couples, and anyone who wants a relaxing day without driving far.
Best for: Swimming, families, easy walking, picnics, lake time, relaxing close to the village.
items.note: Lost Lake gets busy on hot summer days. Go early or later in the day for a calmer visit.

items.name: Paddle on Whistler’s Lakes
paras: Whistler’s lakes are a big part of summer. Alta Lake, Lost Lake, Green Lake, and Nita Lake all offer different ways to enjoy the water.

Alta Lake is especially popular for paddleboarding, canoeing, kayaking, and relaxing at lake parks. Wayside Park and Lakeside Park are useful access points, and Rainbow Park is known for open views across the lake toward the mountains.
Best for: Paddleboarding, canoeing, kayaking, swimming, families, slow summer days.
items.note: Lake water can still be cold early in the season. Wind can also pick up in the afternoon, so beginners should choose calm conditions.

items.name: Try Ziplining or an Adventure Tour
paras: Whistler has many guided adventure tours in summer. Ziplining is one of the most popular, but you may also find rafting, ATV tours, bungee jumping, bear viewing tours, off-road tours, and scenic flights.
These activities are useful if you want adventure but do not have your own gear. They are also good for groups because everything is organized for you.
Best for: Groups, families with older kids, thrill seekers, first-time visitors.
items.note: Check age, height, weight, and safety requirements before booking. Summer tours can sell out.

items.name: Play Golf with Mountain Views
paras: Whistler is a popular summer golf destination, with courses surrounded by mountains, forests, and resort scenery. Golf is a good option if you want an outdoor activity that is active but less intense than hiking or biking.
It is also a good group activity, especially for travelers who want a more relaxed summer day.
Best for: Golfers, groups, couples, scenic summer mornings.
items.note: Book tee times ahead, especially on weekends and peak summer dates.

items.name: Go Bear Viewing or Wildlife Watching
items.alt: A black bear among fireweed
paras: Summer is a good time to join a guided wildlife or bear viewing tour around Whistler. These tours give visitors a safer and more respectful way to learn about local wildlife and habitat.
You may also see birds, squirrels, deer, or other animals while walking trails and parks. Always watch from a distance and never feed wildlife.
Best for: Wildlife lovers, families, photographers, nature-focused travelers.
items.note: Use a guide for bear viewing. Do not approach bears for photos, and keep food and garbage secure.

items.name: Visit Brandywine Falls
paras: Brandywine Falls is one of the best easy side trips near Whistler. It is located south of town along the Sea to Sky Highway and has a short walk to a viewpoint overlooking a tall waterfall in a canyon.
This is a good stop on the drive to or from Whistler, or as part of a slower sightseeing day.
Best for: Waterfall photos, families, short walks, road trips.
items.note: Stay behind barriers and use marked trails. The canyon edges are dangerous.

items.name: Enjoy Summer Patios, Food, and Après-Bike
items.alt: People around an outdoor fire after skiing
paras: Whistler’s food scene is part of the summer experience. After a hike, bike ride, lake day, or tour, the village is full of places to eat, drink, and relax.
Summer patios are especially popular. You can find casual pubs, coffee shops, bakeries, fine dining, family restaurants, cocktail spots, and après-bike energy around the village.
Best for: Food, drinks, groups, couples, nightlife, relaxed evenings.
items.note: Make dinner reservations for popular restaurants, especially on weekends and during peak summer.

items.name: Whistler Blackcomb
items.alt: Whistler and Blackcomb ski runs above the village at dusk
paras: Whistler Blackcomb is the undisputed heavyweight of North American ski resorts, covering over 8,000 acres across two massive mountains. It is a high-alpine kingdom where you can ride a single lift from mossy rainforests at the bottom to windy glaciers at the top.

What makes this place famous is the incredible variety. With over 200 runs, 16 bowls, and 3 glaciers, the area is so big that you can explore for a week and still find new spots. Whether you are watching pros on steep slopes or teaching kids in the Magic Castle, the scale of these mountains is something you have to see to believe.

Location & Access: The resort is divided into two main bases: Whistler Village (access via the Whistler Village Gondola or Fitzsimmons Express) and the Upper Village (access via the Blackcomb Gondola). Both mountains are seamlessly connected mid-mountain by the Peak 2 Peak Gondola.

items.name: Peak 2 Peak Gondola
items.alt: A child in a red gondola cabin with skis, mountains behind
paras: The Peak 2 Peak is a high-speed gondola system that links the alpine hubs of Whistler Mountain and Blackcomb Mountain, letting skiers and sightseers glide across the deep valley between them in roughly 11 minutes. The full span stretches about 4.4 km (2.7 miles), and it famously holds the world record for the longest unsupported span between two cable towers, 3.024 km.

Even more jaw-dropping is the height: at its highest point, the gondola hangs about 436 metres (1,427 feet) above the valley floor, delivering a true floating over the wilderness feeling. On a clear day, you can see the volcanic spire of Black Tusk, the sprawling Fitzsimmons Creek below, and the ancient glaciers that carved this landscape.

Location & Access: The Peak 2 Peak terminals are located at Roundhouse Lodge (Whistler Mountain) and Rendezvous Lodge (Blackcomb Mountain). You reach them by taking the main gondolas up from Whistler Village (Whistler Gondola) or the Upper Village (Blackcomb Gondola). The Peak 2 Peak Gondola is open year-round, but weather conditions can affect operations, particularly during the winter months.

items.name: Olympic Rings (Whistler Olympic Plaza)
paras: The Olympic Rings at the Whistler Olympic Plaza are the definitive symbol of the town’s 2010 Winter Games legacy. While they are technically a photo-op, the plaza they sit in is really the town square of the Village. It’s a massive, open-air green space (or snow space, depending on when you visit) where the energy of the town shifts from adrenaline-fueled mountain sports to community chill.

What makes this spot special is the backdrop. You’ve got the giant rings in the foreground and the towering peaks of Whistler and Blackcomb looming right behind them. It’s the kind of place where you’ll see kids running on the grass in the summer, or locals playing a game of pond hockey on the outdoor rink in the winter.

Location & Access: You’ll find the rings at the north end of the Village Stroll in Whistler Olympic Plaza. If you’re walking from the main gondola base, just follow the Stroll all the way past the shops; you can’t miss the giant open field and the mountain views.

items.name: Whistler Inukshuk
items.alt: The Whistler Inukshuk against the Black Tusk
paras: The Whistler Inukshuk is much more than just a stone statue; it is a powerful symbol of Northern culture and a permanent legacy of the 2010 Winter Games. Standing tall at the very top of the world, this traditional Inuit stone landmark was historically used as a navigational aid or to mark sacred ground. Here in the Coast Mountains, it serves as a silent guardian overlooking the vast, snow-capped wilderness.

What makes this particular Inukshuk so special is its placement. Perched on a rocky ridge at the summit, it creates a dramatic contrast between man-made heritage and the raw, jagged peaks of the Garibaldi Ranges. Standing next to it, you get a humbling sense of scale, it feels like you’re at the edge of the map. On a bluebird day, the grey stones pop against the deep blue sky, making it arguably the most meaningful photo-op in the entire province.

Location & Access: The most famous Inukshuk is located at the summit of Whistler Mountain, right near the top of the Peak Express Chairlift. To get there, you’ll take the Whistler Village Gondola to the Roundhouse Lodge, walk a short distance to the Peak Express, and ride the open-air chair to the very top.

items.name: Brandywine Falls Provincial Park
paras: Brandywine Falls is that wow moment you usually find on the cover of a travel magazine. It’s a spectacular 70-metre (230-foot) waterfall that plunges over a sheer basalt cliff into a perfectly round volcanic bowl. What makes it so striking isn't just the height, but the way the water has carved through layers of ancient lava flows over thousands of years, leaving behind a rugged, prehistoric-looking canyon.

It’s the ultimate low effort, high reward stop. A flat, easy 15-minute walk through a lush forest brings you to a viewing platform that makes you feel tiny against the roar of the water. On a sunny afternoon, you’ll almost always see a rainbow shimmering in the mist at the base of the falls, hence the name Brandywine. It’s the perfect place to stretch your legs and get your first real taste of the Sea to Sky wilderness.

Location & Access: You’ll find the entrance right off Highway 99, about 15 minutes (20km) south of Whistler Village. There is a large, well-marked parking lot, and the trail to the falls is a wide, gravel path that is easy for almost anyone to navigate.

items.name: The Black Tusk
paras: The Black Tusk is the unmistakable crown of the Garibaldi Ranges, a jagged, black volcanic spire that looks like a giant tooth jutting out from a sea of white glaciers. It’s easily the most recognizable landmark in the Whistler skyline. This isn't just another mountain; it’s the core of an ancient volcano that erupted roughly 170,000 years ago. Over time, the softer outer rock eroded away, leaving behind this dramatic, dark basalt plug that stands in stark contrast to the surrounding green valleys and blue alpine lakes.

For the Squamish People, the Tusk is known as the Landing Place of the Thunderbird. It carries a heavy sense of mystery and power that you feel the moment you see it from a distance. Whether you are staring at it from a gondola or standing on its base, the Tusk feels ancient, imposing, and completely wild. It’s the ultimate North Star for hikers and photographers in the region.

Location & Access: The Black Tusk is located within Garibaldi Provincial Park. To see it up close, most hikers start at the Rubble Creek trailhead, about a 25-minute drive south of Whistler. To see it without the 11-hour hike, simply take the Whistler Village Gondola to the summit, it looms large on the southern horizon from almost any high-alpine viewpoint.

items.name: Whistler Sliding Centre
items.alt: The lit ice track at the Whistler Sliding Centre
paras: The Whistler Sliding Centre is where the high-octane legacy of the 2010 Winter Olympics truly lives on. Tucked onto the side of Blackcomb Mountain, this is the fastest ice track in the world, a serpentine ribbon of concrete and ice where athletes hit speeds that most of us only reach on the highway. It’s a place of incredible intensity; standing beside the track while a sled thunders past is an experience that vibrates right through your chest.

What’s truly unique about the Sliding Centre is that it isn’t just for pros. It is one of the very few Olympic venues globally where regular people can actually jump in a sled and experience the g-force for themselves. Whether you’re watching world-class lugers train or bracing yourself for a bobsleigh run, there’s an electric, competitive energy here that you won’t find anywhere else in the valley.

Location & Access: You’ll find the Centre at 4910 Glacier Lane, just above the Upper Village. You can reach it via a quick 5-minute drive or by taking the Excalibur Gondola (which is free for foot passengers) to the first stop and walking about 10 minutes up the hill.

items.name: Whistler Mountain Bike Park
paras: Whistler Mountain Bike Park is a world-renowned biking destination that draws enthusiasts from around the globe. When the snow melts, the ski runs transform into a massive, gravity-fed playground with over 80 kilometers of trails winding through four distinct mountain zones. It’s a high-energy landscape where you’ll see everyone from world-class professionals catching massive air to families tentatively navigating their first forest loamy paths.

What makes the park legendary is its flow. The trail builders here are artists; they’ve created everything from Easy Tiger, a gentle introduction to downhill, to A-Line, arguably the most famous jump trail on the planet. Even if you don’t ride, standing at the base and watching riders fly off the final drops into the Village is a spectator sport in its own right. It’s loud, dusty, and absolutely exhilarating, a place where the adrenaline of winter is kept alive all summer long.

Location & Access: The main hub is at the Whistler Village Base, where you load the Fitzsimmons Express or the Whistler Village Gondola. You can also access the higher Creekside Zone via the Creekside Gondola, which offers a quieter, local feel with some of the best technical trails in the park.

items.name: Cloudraker Skybridge
items.alt: The Cloudraker Skybridge across a rocky ridge
paras: The Cloudraker Skybridge, often simply called the Whistler Suspension Bridge, is one of those take your breath away experiences that stays with you long after you’ve headed back down the mountain. Stretching 130 metres (427 feet) from Whistler Peak to the West Ridge, it hangs right over the legendary Whistler Bowl. It’s not just a bridge; it’s a high-altitude thrill ride where you’re suspended in the open air, feeling the mountain breeze and staring down into a dizzying alpine abyss.

What makes it truly unique is the engineering and the sheer height. Standing at over 2,000 metres (nearly 7,000 feet) above sea level, you get a 360-degree view that includes the jagged Tantalus Range and the icy glaciers of Blackcomb. The bridge has a slight sway to it, which adds to the adrenaline, but it’s the Raven’s Eye, a cantilevered viewing platform at the far end, that really steals the show. It extends out over the cliff edge, making you feel like you’re literally floating above the mountain peaks.

Location & Access: The bridge is located at the very top of Whistler Mountain. To get there, take the Whistler Village Gondola to the Roundhouse Lodge, then walk to the Peak Express Chairlift. Once you get off the chair at the summit, the bridge entrance is just a few steps away.

items.name: Joffre Lakes Provincial Park
items.alt: A turquoise lake under a forested peak
paras: Joffre Lakes is the kind of place that looks like a Photoshop filter come to life. It’s a string of three glacier-fed lakes, Lower, Middle, and Upper, each one a more impossible shade of turquoise than the last. This vibrant Gatorade blue comes from silt (rock flour) suspended in the glacial meltwater, reflecting the sunlight in a way that’s almost blindingly bright. It’s a rugged, high-alpine landscape where ancient glaciers hang off the peaks right above you.

What makes this hike so iconic is the progression. You start in the dense, cool forest and work your way up to the Matier Glacier, which feeds the lakes. It’s a steep climb in sections, but the moment you break through the trees at Middle Lake and see that famous log floating in the blue water, all the effort feels worth it. It’s a quintessential British Columbia experience, raw and beautiful.

Location & Access: Joffre Lakes is located about an hour’s drive (60km) north of Whistler, just past the town of Pemberton. The trailhead has a large parking lot right off Highway 99 (the Sea to Sky Highway). Unlike the Village attractions, you’ll definitely need a car or a booked shuttle to get here.

items.name: Squamish Lil'wat Cultural Centre
items.alt: Carved cedar drums at the Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre
paras: The Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre (SLCC) is the soulful heart of the valley. While the rest of Whistler often feels like a fast-paced playground, this center invites you to slow down and connect with the land’s original high-alpine culture. It is a stunning, light-filled space designed to evoke a traditional Squamish Longhouse and a Lil’wat Earth House (Istken). Here, the history isn't just kept in glass cases; it’s lived and shared through the voices of the people who have called these mountains home since time immemorial.

What makes the SLCC so special is the atmosphere of genuine hospitality. As soon as you walk in, you’re greeted by the smell of cedar and the sound of hand-drums. It’s an immersive journey through the distinct traditions of the Squamish and Lil’wat Nations. From the massive 40-foot dugout canoes to the intricate hand-woven cedar baskets, every piece tells a story of survival, artistry, and a deep respect for the natural world.

Location & Access: You’ll find the center at 4584 Blackcomb Way in the Upper Village. It’s a beautiful, flat 10-minute walk from the main Village Stroll or a quick ride on the free #5 Upper Village shuttle.

items.name: Audain Art Museum
items.alt: The snowy approach to the Audain Art Museum
paras: The Audain Art Museum is Whistler’s quiet masterpiece, a stunning architectural gem tucked into a grove of towering trees between the Village and the Upper Village. While the mountains offer adrenaline, the Audain offers a deep, soul-stirring look at the cultural history of British Columbia. The building itself is a work of art, a dark, minimalist structure elevated on stilts to protect the forest floor and withstand the heavy local snowfall.

The museum houses one of the world’s most significant collections of Northwest Coast First Nations masks, alongside iconic works by Emily Carr and contemporary Canadian masters. The lighting is low and intimate, designed to make the intricate cedar carvings feel like they are floating in the dark.

Location & Access: You’ll find the museum at 4350 Blackcomb Way. It’s located right along the Village Stroll, just a three-minute walk from the Olympic Plaza. If you’re coming from the Upper Village, it’s an easy, flat walk across the Fitzsimmons Creek bridge.

items.name: Whistler Olympic Park
items.alt: Fat bikers riding through snowy forest
paras: Whistler Olympic Park is the quiet, expansive counterpart to the bustling downhill slopes. Located in the beautiful Callaghan Valley, this 2010 Olympic venue hosted the Nordic events, cross-country skiing, biathlon, and ski jumping. Today, it’s a world-class winter and summer playground that feels more like a serene wilderness retreat than a high-traffic resort.

What makes this place stand out is the scale of the landscape. With over 90 kilometers of groomed trails winding through ancient forests and wide-open meadows, it’s where you go to find some breathing room. In the winter, the silence of the valley is broken only by the sound of skis on corduroy; in the summer, it transforms into a lush haven for hiking and bear-watching.

Location & Access: The Park is located at 5 Callaghan Valley Road, about a 30-minute drive south of Whistler Village. Since there is no shuttle service in 2026, you’ll need a rental car or a local taxi to get there. The drive itself is spectacular, often offering better chances of spotting local wildlife than the main highway.

items.name: The Whistler Train Wreck Trail
paras: The Whistler Train Wreck is easily the town’s most unique cultural landmark, a bizarre and beautiful blend of industrial history and modern street art. In 1956, a freighter train derailed south of town, and seven massive boxcars were wedged so deeply into the old-growth forest that they were simply left behind. Over the decades, local graffiti artists transformed these rusting metal giants into a vibrant, ever-evolving outdoor gallery.

The setting is pure West Coast: towering cedars, mossy forest floors, and the rushing turquoise water of the Cheakamus River. To reach the cars, you’ll cross a stunning suspension bridge that offers a bird’s-eye view of the white-water rapids below. It feels like stepping into a post-apocalyptic fairy tale where nature is slowly reclaiming heavy machinery, and it’s one of the few places in Whistler where the vibe is more gritty and bohemian than polished and resort-like.

Location & Access: The trailhead is located in the Creekside/Cheakamus area at the end of Jane Lakes Road. It’s about a 10-minute drive south of Whistler Village. There is a designated parking lot, and the hike is a relatively flat, 2-km (1.2-mile) round trip that takes about an hour at a leisurely pace.

items.name: Whistler Museum
paras: The Whistler Museum is a charming, deep dive into the town’s transformation from a rugged fishing outpost to a world-class Olympic destination. While the surrounding Village is shiny and modern, the museum keeps the old Whistler spirit alive. It’s packed with eccentric mountain memorabilia, from vintage ski gear that looks terrifyingly primitive to stories of the early pioneers who fought to put this valley on the map long before the first chairlift ever turned.

Location & Access: You’ll find the museum at 4333 Main Street, right next to the Whistler Public Library and just a few steps from the Olympic Plaza. It’s an easy walk from anywhere in the main Village.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

items.name: Whistler Public Library
paras: The Whistler Public Library, affectionately known as the Whistler Cabin, is far from your typical quiet book depository. It is an architectural masterpiece and the community’s favorite living room. Designed with high vaulted ceilings, massive Douglas Fir beams, and floor-to-ceiling windows, the building captures the essence of a modern mountain lodge. It was built to the "LEED Gold" environmental standard, making it as sustainable as it is beautiful.

What makes this spot a must-visit isn't just the books; it’s the atmosphere. Whether the snow is dumping outside or the summer sun is hitting the Olympic Plaza next door, the library offers a warm, peaceful sanctuary with some of the best mountain views in the Village. It’s where locals come to remote-work, travelers come to recharge their devices, and families gather for some low-key downtime between adventures.

Location & Access: You’ll find the library at 4329 Main Street, right in the heart of the Village. It sits directly across the courtyard from the Whistler Museum and overlooks the open greenspace of Whistler Olympic Plaza.

items.name: Whistler Art Galleries
paras: Whistler’s art scene is a vibrant, mountain-town mix of high-end luxury and rugged, local creativity. While the big museums get the headlines, the private Whistler Art Galleries scattered throughout the Village are where you can actually get your hands on a piece of the Pacific Northwest. These spaces range from sleek, modern showrooms to cozy mountain studios, featuring everything from hyper-realistic landscape paintings to massive bronze sculptures and traditional Indigenous carvings.

The variety is what makes gallery-hopping here so engaging. It’s a culture of mountain-inspired art that reflects the scale of the peaks and the textures of the forest, offering a sophisticated way to experience the valley when you’re off the slopes or trails.

Location & Access: Most galleries are clustered along the Village Stroll, in the Upper Village (inside the Fairmont Chateau Whistler), or tucked into the Hilton and Westin resort lobbies. They are all easily reachable on foot within a 15-minute walk of the main gondola base.

items.name: Lost Lake
items.alt: A forested lake with a small island
paras: Lost Lake is the local’s favorite sanctuary, offering a serene escape just minutes from the high-energy pulse of Whistler Village. Nestled within 525 acres of pristine parkland, the lake is a tranquil mirror reflecting the surrounding Douglas firs and the peaks of Blackcomb. In the summer, it’s the go-to spot for sunbathing on sandy beaches and swimming in the calm, crisp water; in the winter, it transforms into a world-class Nordic center with groomed cross-country ski and snowshoe trails that look like something out of a holiday card.

What makes Lost Lake truly special is its accessibility. You don’t need a mountain pass or a rugged 4x4 to get here, just a pair of sneakers or a cruiser bike. It’s a place that balances wild and convenient perfectly, allowing you to go from a morning coffee in the Village to a secluded lakeside forest trail in under 15 minutes.

Location & Access: You can reach Lost Lake via a flat, scenic 1.5-km (0.9-mile) walk along the Valley Trail starting from the Village. During the summer, a free shuttle bus (Route #8) runs regularly from the Village Gate Boulevard to the lakefront.

items.name: Valley Trail
items.alt: Cyclists on the Valley Trail beside the lake
paras: The Valley Trail is the scenic, car-free artery that connects the entire Whistler valley. Stretching over 46 kilometers (28 miles), this paved network links every major neighborhood, five shimmering lakes, and countless parks. While the mountains get all the glory, the Valley Trail is where the real Whistler happens. It’s a place where you can glide past golf courses, cross rushing glacial rivers on wooden bridges, and wind through ancient cedar groves without ever having to worry about traffic.

It’s a multi-seasonal gem; in the summer, it's a highway for cruiser bikes and skateboards, while in the winter, many sections are cleared or groomed, allowing for a unique perspective of the snow-covered valley floor.

Location & Access: The trail has entry points throughout the town, but the most popular hubs are in Whistler Village (near the Olympic Plaza), Upper Village, and Creekside. You can pick up a trail map at the Visitor Centre or simply follow the yellow directional signs located at every major junction.

items.name: Alexander Falls
items.alt: A waterfall dropping through forest
paras: Alexander Falls is the quiet giant of the Whistler area, a spectacular, multi-tiered waterfall that drops a sheer 43 meters (141 feet) into the Madeley Creek valley. While Brandywine Falls gets the highway crowds, Alexander Falls offers a more serene, off-the-beaten-path experience. The water cascades over three distinct steps of volcanic basalt rock, creating a wide, curtain-like effect that is especially thunderous during the spring snowmelt.

What makes it a standout is the viewing experience. Unlike many falls where you have to hike for miles to get a glimpse, Alexander Falls features a large, paved viewing platform located right at the top of the canyon. It provides a perfect, straight-on perspective of the water’s plunge against a backdrop of dense old-growth forest. It feels grand, wild, and incredibly peaceful, making it a favorite for those who want a big mountain view without the big mountain effort.

Location & Access: The falls are located in the Callaghan Valley, about a 20-minute drive south of Whistler Village. To get there, turn off Highway 99 onto Callaghan Valley Road (follow signs for Whistler Olympic Park). The parking lot for the Alexander Falls Forest Service Site is located on the left side of the road, just before you reach the main gate of the Olympic Park.

items.name: Cheakamus Lake Trail
items.alt: A glassy lake with snow peaks behind
paras: The Cheakamus Lake Trail is the perfect antidote to the steep, leg-burning climbs usually associated with Whistler. Located within the magnificent Garibaldi Provincial Park, this trail winds through some of the most impressive old-growth forests in the valley, featuring massive Douglas firs and ancient cedars that dwarf everything in their path. The payoff is a stunning, 7-km long lake filled with vivid, turquoise glacial water, framed by the dramatic, snow-capped peaks of the Fitzsimmons Range.

What makes this hike a local favorite is its accessibility and high reward for low effort. The trail is relatively flat, making it one of the few places in the region where you can experience true backcountry wilderness without a 1,000-meter vertical climb.

Location & Access: The trailhead is located at the end of Cheakamus Lake Road, a forest service road that begins just south of the Cheakamus Crossing neighborhood. It’s about a 15-minute drive from Whistler Village. The final 6 km of the drive is on a gravel road that can be bumpy, but it is typically manageable for most standard vehicles.

items.name: Alta Lake Park
paras: Alta Lake is the historical heart of Whistler and its largest body of water. Long before the first ski lift was ever bolted into the mountainside, this was a summer retreat for fishing and lodge life. Today, it serves as the valley’s ultimate aquatic playground, framed by panoramic views of both Whistler and Blackcomb mountains. Unlike the glacier-fed lakes that stay bone-chillingly cold, Alta Lake’s shallower waters warm up enough in the summer to make it the go-to destination for swimming, paddleboarding, and kayaking.

Alta Lake is unique because of the different personalities found along its shores. It features three distinct parks, Rainbow, Lakeside, and Wayside, each offering a different view of the valley. Whether you want a sandy beach for a family barbecue, a quiet spot to launch a canoe, or a chance to see historic pioneer cabins, the lake provides a great escape from the busy Village.

Location & Access: Alta Lake is located about 2 km (1.2 miles) west of Whistler Village. It is most easily accessed via the Valley Trail, a scenic 20-minute walk or 10-minute bike ride. Each park has its own small parking lot, but these fill up quickly on sunny days.

items.name: Cheakamus River
items.alt: A glassy lake with snow peaks behind
paras: The Cheakamus River is the powerful, bright teal lifeblood of the Whistler valley. Fed by melting glaciers, the river shows off the raw beauty of the Pacific Northwest. It thunders through deep canyons and flows under giant, moss-covered trees. Its striking color comes from fine rock dust ground down by glaciers, making the water look like it is glowing against the dark forest.

Depending on where you are, you might see calm, quiet pools or crashing whitewater rapids. It is a perfect spot for everyone, from brave rafters and kayakers to hikers looking for a peaceful riverside walk.

Location & Access: The river runs south of Whistler Village. The best access points are in the Cheakamus Crossing neighborhood, via the Whistler Train Wreck trailhead, or from the Cheakamus Lake Road parking areas. Many sections are easily reached by a 10-15 minute drive from the main Village.

items.name: Wedgemount Lake
items.alt: A turquoise lake below bare mountains
paras: Wedgemount Lake is often called the ultimate Whistler hike, a tough, steep climb that leads to a dramatic, otherworldly landscape. Located high in Garibaldi Provincial Park, the lake is a bright, milky turquoise and sits right at the base of the massive Wedgemount Glacier. This is not a casual walk; it is a rugged ascent through thick forests and rock fields that brings you face-to-face with the edge of a glacier.

The scenery here is legendary. Once you finish the final, difficult climb, you are rewarded with views of jagged mountain peaks. The area is incredibly quiet, with the silence only broken by the sound of moving ice or waterfalls crashing down the rocks. It is a place of extreme beauty that requires great effort, perfect for those who want to see the wild side of the mountains.

Location & Access: The trailhead is located about 13 km (8 miles) north of Whistler Village. You’ll turn off Highway 99 onto a gravel forest service road. While most cars can make it to the lower parking lot, a 4x4 is recommended for the final stretch to the upper lot.

items.name: Ancient Cedars Trail
items.alt: A hiker passing giant cedars
paras: The Ancient Cedars Trail is a journey back in time, leading you to a hidden grove of giants that have stood for over 900 years. While much of the valley was logged in the early 20th century, this pocket of old-growth forest remained untouched. Walking among these massive Western Red Cedars, some measuring over 3 metres in diameter, is a humbling experience.
